title: Egress Pathfinding + Private VPC Quant & Batching Lab
summary: Lab-style deep dive focused on private VPC egress pathfinding, DNS split-horizon, NAT hairpinning, and how quantized model variants interact with KV cache hit rates and batching. Agreed to run a 24-hr replay of production traffic to measure prefix-cache hit ratio and tail latency with RBAC-enabled PrivateLink endpoints.
topics: PrivateLink ENI behavior and cross-AZ pathing
Egress NAT vs Transit Gateway for inference traffic
Split-horizon DNS impact on resolver latency
KV cache warmstart and prefix caching with quantized models
Batching latencies and head-of-line blocking in steady-state vs burst
SNI/mTLS egress proxy design for on-prem KMS calls
action_items: Rajesh Iyer - Share VPC route tables and NAT GW metrics (bytes/flows) - due 2028-11-20
Marco Nguyen - Prepare a replay harness for 24-hr traffic subset + recommended kvcache tuning - due 2028-11-17
Sofia Patel - Send security artifact pack (SOC2 attestation, KMS integration notes) and pricing ranges - due 2028-11-15

next_steps: Schedule replay kickoff meeting with Poise infra (30m) - target 2028-11-16
Run quantized model variant A/B during replay to compare kvcache hit and TTL behavior
Exchange pinhole firewall rules and suggested security group templates for PrivateLink ENIs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-11-13
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel, Marco Nguyen, Eileen Park (Redwood) / Lydia Chen, Rajesh Iyer, Maya Torres, Devon Kumar (Poise)

Summary (auto): Quick lab to map egress routes from Poise's private VPC to Redwood's PrivateLink endpoints and to surface networking causes of KV cache misses when switching to a quantized model.

[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Lydia (Poise): Lydia here. Rajesh, Maya, Devon also on.
[00:20] Marco (Redwood SE): Marco NG, SE. Eileen here as well. We'll focus on egress pathfinding and a short replay.
[00:35] Rajesh (Poise SRE): Sounds good. We saw tail spikes last week when we flipped to the 4-bit quantized model for cheaper tokens. Trying to understand if it's network or runtime.
[00:48] Sofia: Right. From our side we've seen two categories: KV-cache warming and network-induced replays. We'll try to tease them apart.

[01:10] Marco: Quick architecture recap—Poise has PrivateLink endpoints in three AZs with ENIs in each; traffic leaves via a NAT GW in our egress subnet for external KMS and telemetry. Is that accurate?
[01:28] Devon (Poise Net): Yes, we have an active NAT in AZ-a and standby in AZ-b, and a TGW for cross-account routing. PrivateLink sits in a dedicated subnet with very restrictive SGs.
[01:40] Marco: Good. Two quick pain points we often see: asymmetric routing because ENI sources differ and hairpin NAT when pods talk to PrivateLink ENIs in the same VPC but different AZ, which can add 10-40ms depending on path.
[01:58] Rajesh: We're seeing about 30–60ms extra tail on some requests; that's consistent with what you said. Also TTL for kvcache entries seems shorter after quantized model switch. Not sure why.

[02:20] Eileen (Redwood SE): Two hypotheses: 1) quantized models change token distribution so prefix cache hit-rate drops because prompts diverge, 2) retry/timeout thresholds in your egress path cause repeated key fetches to KMS or redis, invalidating cache.
[02:40] Maya (Poise Sec): On KMS — we route to an on-prem HSM through an outbound TLS proxy, there is mutual TLS and an SNI-based front. Those calls add jitter.

[03:05] Marco: OK, let's map request flow with numbers. Example: request enters Poise VPC -> pod -> egress through NAT -> Public KMS (or proxy) OR -> PrivateLink directly to Redwood endpoint (if route table points there). If the PrivateLink route isn't preferred, traffic can hairpin out to NAT and back in which inflates latency and can split flows across AZs causing kv cache sharding inefficiencies.

[03:40] Lydia: Is there an easy audit to show hairpinning? We have VPC FlowLogs but they're noisy.
[03:50] Marco: VPC flow logs + ENI source/dest correlation. Also traceroute from pod namespace to privatelink IP and capture socket-level SNI. A simple tcpdump on the pod before and after the ENI helps.

[04:12] Rajesh: We can run tcpdump but our compliance team is sensitive. We'll coordinate with Maya.

[04:30] Sofia: On the kvcache side, our runtime keeps prefix caches per-model variant. Quantization changes the tokenization alignment slightly which can reduce exact prefix matches — especially with our 4-bit int8 like variants. That means more KV lookups until the cache warms.

[05:00] Marco: Right — quantization isn't supposed to change semantics, but subtle output differences + prompt continuation strategies affect hit-rate. If you add even a microsecond of network jitter and a retry policy that replays the request, you multiply the load and thrash the cache.

[05:25] Devon: Can you explain the retry policy bit? Where's the replay happening?
[05:30] Eileen: If the proxy or NAT sees a transient error, the client may reconnect and the runtime restarts generation which causes KV cache to be cold for that generation attempt. We recommend idempotent client behavior with a single-server-side retry window to avoid double work.

[06:00] Rajesh: Our client library is bundled with a 2s connect timeout and 3s overall request timeout. Maybe that's too aggressive.

[06:10] Marco: For interactive workloads we usually use a longer initial handshake timeout (5–8s) and streaming-level keepalives. For high throughput batch non-streaming, shorter timeouts work, but you must watch the retry amplification.

[06:40] Sofia: Let's pivot to DNS. Split-horizon DNS sometimes routes privilege traffic to private resolver in your VPC which is slower if it forwards to on-prem. That adds 15–100ms depending on resolver chain.

[06:55] Maya: Our resolver chain sends unknown queries to on-prem, yes — primarily for audit. Is forwarding unavoidable?
[07:02] Marco: Not always. You can cache Redwood's private endpoint answers locally on the node resolver (nscd/Unbound) to avoid the forward. Or add explicit host entries as a last resort for stability.

[07:20] Rajesh: We can add Unbound but we need to validate TTLs and avoid stale records.

[07:32] Marco: TTL tuning matters — short TTLs cause repeated resolutions during bursts, adding latency. Increasing TTL for Redwood endpoints to something like 300s reduces chatter. We also support mutual TLS SNI for egress so you can pin to a region-specific load balancer.

[08:00] Sofia: Quick demo idea — Marco will show a replay run with metrics: p99 latency, kvcache hit-rate, number of KMS calls, and number of retransmits.

[08:15] Marco: I'll walk through a baseline we ran in staging.

[08:20] [screen share noises] Marco: In the baseline, median sequence length 64 tokens, batching window 25ms, continuous batching enabled. We saw kvcache hit-rate drop from 78% to 46% when switching to quantized variant B, and p99 latency went from 180ms to 310ms on same infra during a 5k rps burst.

[09:02] Lydia: That's big. Were those numbers network-limited?
[09:06] Marco: Mixed. About 40% of extra tail was network (hairpin and DNS), 60% was runtime (cache churn + longer decode times on quantized path because we fell back to a slower kernel for some ops). The runtime fallback occurs when vector instructions don't match the quant profile for that layer.

[09:30] Rajesh: Is there a knob to prefer a faster kernel even at small quality loss?
[09:35] Eileen: Yes — Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles per-layer vs global. We can push a profile that prefers a faster op path for tail-critical routes. That's part of the replay we'll propose.

[10:00] Sofia: Networking mitigations?
[10:04] Marco: A few practical ones: 1) Make PrivateLink route table the preferred route for the egress CIDR so you avoid NAT hairpin, 2) Pre-warm kvcache by replaying cold prefixes during off-peak, 3) Increase DNS TTLs for our endpoints or run a local caching resolver, 4) Tune client timeouts to avoid replay amplification.

[10:35] Devon: About point 1 — if we change route preference, does that affect other services that need NAT?
[10:40] Marco: It can. We recommend using more-specific route entries for Redwood endpoints (prefix length /32 or /28) so they route to PrivateLink only while other egress continues via NAT. That keeps separation.

[11:00] Rajesh: What about security groups on the ENI? We're restricted to narrow SGs which may block certain return paths. Could SG state cause asymmetric routing?
[11:12] Marco: SGs are stateful so return traffic should be fine. Asymmetric routing typically comes from route table differences across subnets and TGW attachments. But overly-restrictive SGs combined with DNAT can result in unexpected resets. We'll review the SG rules in the replay packet capture.

[11:40] Maya: On the KMS calls, our mTLS proxy currently does DNS over TLS to on-prem resolver; that path added ~45ms. Can Redwood allow a regional KMS endpoint over PrivateLink?

[11:55] Sofia: We have PrivateLink options for KMS in some regions but not all. We'll document current coverage and alternatives (HSM co-locate or KMS caching).

[12:10] Eileen: Also consider a local short-lived secret cache for non-PII keys to cut KMS round trips; we can recommend TTL strategies and rotation cadence.

[12:30] Marco: Back to batching: with continuous batching, small tail latency wins if batch windows are tuned properly. We saw 25ms window gave good throughput but allowed more head-of-line blocking under bursty traffic; increasing to 40ms smoothed out variance but raised median slightly. It's a tradeoff.

[12:58] Lydia: How do you measure head-of-line?
[13:02] Marco: Look at service queue time histograms per model-route and compare percent of tokens delayed beyond window. Also monitor per-worker KV cache miss rates correlated with queue length.

[13:30] Rajesh: If cache misses spike, does the runtime fallback to single-thread decode?
[13:35] Eileen: No, not single-thread necessarily, but there are kernel choices that are scalar-fallbacks; they run slower. We also sometimes disable fused multihead kernels on quantized bits which impacts throughput.

[14:00] Sofia: Let's record a concrete pilot: Marco will run replay with two quant profiles (A = quality-first, B = latency-first) and show per-route p50/p95/p99, kvcache hit-rate, KMS calls, and DNS resolution latency. Poise will provide 6 hours of sampled traffic and NAT/GW metrics.

[14:30] Rajesh: We'll redact PII from logs and share route tables. Expect to drop them into the secure S3 bucket.

[14:45] Marco: For the replay harness, we need: sample of request/response pairs (not full prompts), client timeout settings, and the egress path (Privatelink IPs, NAT IPs). We'll synthesize token lengths to match production distribution.

[15:05] Maya: Security question — if we pre-warm cache, are we sending real customer prompts to Redwood? That's not allowed.

[15:12] Sofia: We'll only use hashed prefixes and synthetic delimiters. The warmstart can be performed with synthetic prefixes that preserve length and token distribution without PII. We'll document the sanitization process.

[15:30] Devon: One last network item — MTU mismatch between on-prem VPN and AWS ENIs caused fragmentation and added ~20ms in a prior engagement. Should we check MTU?

[15:40] Marco: Yes, check MTU end-to-end and enable path MTU discovery on your proxy. Also verify jumbo frames if using SR-IOV.

[16:00] Sofia: Great — let's recap next steps and owners. (recap)...

[16:10] Lydia: Quick clarifying Q: if we opt for PrivateLink-only egress for inference traffic, how do we handle logs/telemetry that need internet?
[16:22] Eileen: Split routing: create explicit route prefixes for telemetry endpoints via NAT and keep inference endpoints via PrivateLink. Or send telemetry over a separate VPC peering path that has different policies.

[16:45] Rajesh: Thanks everyone.
[16:50] Devon: We'll get route tables and sample logs to you by Friday.

[51:58] Sofia: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the replay plan. Bye.
